## Context

Milestone 5b: Mustur knows who is asking. Invitation, passkey, session and role, all held beside the record log rather than in it, because who may read the records is not itself a record. Four surfaces, drawn after they were built and rebuilt from the drawings.

## Done means

An invitation is a one-time link, printed once and stored only as a hash; it expires in 24 hours and is spent only after the passkey verifies. A person invited to an address registers a passkey and is signed in by the act of registering. Signing out and back in needs nothing typed: the browser offers whichever passkey is scoped to this site and the server never asks who is asking. A passkey is refused on any other relying party, which is the property that makes it unphishable. A challenge is spent once. A whole captured response replayed a second time is refused. A device lost is a device replaced: a second invitation to the same address lands on the same account, keeping its identifier, its other passkeys and its role. The last passkey on an account cannot be removed, and somebody else's passkey cannot be removed at all. A role is per project. An account with a role only on another project reads nothing here. A reader reaches every reading surface and none that types into a running agent, including by GET. Only an owner may invite, change a role or disable somebody, refused by the handler and not only hidden in the page. The only owner cannot demote or disable themselves, and finds out at the control rather than from a banner. Disabling somebody ends their sessions immediately rather than leaving them alive until they expire. Enforcement is a flag, off by default, because turning it on before the owner holds a passkey locks the owner out of their own service. The first owner is made by the machine, since there is nobody to send the first invitation. Four surfaces: sign in, accept an invitation, account, people. Each carries script only where WebAuthn forces it. They were built before they were drawn and then rebuilt from the drawings, which the risks below record rather than smooth over.

## Verified against

Tests, including the ceremony itself against a virtual authenticator written for this unit — 200 lines of ES256 and CBOR that speak this server's protocol correctly. Until it existed every test started after the passkey, with a session cookie minted by hand, and a comment in guard_test.go said the ceremony needed a browser. It does not; it needs a correct client. What it drives, on the real endpoints in the real order: invited, registered, signed out, recognised (TestAnInvitedPersonRegistersASignsOutAndIsRecognised). A replayed assertion refused, because the ceremony is deleted when it is read (TestAChallengeCannotBeSpentTwice). A passkey signed for another relying party refused, with a control run through the same code differing only in that field, so the refusal attributes to something (TestAPasskeyForAnotherSiteIsRefused). A lost device replaced onto the same account with its role intact (TestALostDeviceIsReplacedWithoutLosingTheAccount), and a second passkey added from the account page, either one signing in (TestASecondPasskeyIsAddedFromTheAccountPage). The cross-account test earns its name the hard way: it passed with Mustur's own handle check deleted, because the library's session check was refusing underneath it. It now asserts which refusal it got and fails when that check goes. The guard, separately: a reader refused the two agent surfaces even to read; an account with a role elsewhere refused; a stranger redirected on a GET and refused on a POST, since a redirect answering a POST reads as success; sign-in, its script and an invitation link public, or nobody could ever get an account. MUS-F-0026 was found by a comment on a drawing rather than by any test, and now has one that fails without the fix. What no test here proves is a real authenticator: a phone, a fingerprint, a browser. That is the owner's to try, as 2c's last sentence was.

## Risks

Nothing in this unit is deployed. The running service has no --origin and no --accounts, so the surfaces exist and answer nowhere. Turning enforcement on before the owner holds a passkey locks the owner out. The order is: deploy with --origin, make the first owner, register a passkey, then --accounts. Cloudflare Access stays in front throughout and its removal is a separate act the owner judges, not part of this milestone's verdict (MUS-Q-0039). The account page now carries script, which takes the scripted surfaces from three to four (MUS-Q-0047). Everything on it except the ceremony works without. The four surfaces were built before they were drawn — the fourth time this repository has done that, and the pattern is a finding of its own rather than four separate ones. They were drawn afterwards under MUS-Q-0043 and rebuilt from the drawings, which is remediation and not the same as having drawn them first. The guard knows one project. A second project would need it to ask a different question, which is a value to change rather than a rule. Sessions live 30 days and are not bound to a device beyond the cookie; a stolen cookie is a signed-in browser until it is signed out or the account is disabled. A virtual authenticator is a correct client, not a real one. It says nothing about attestation, about hardware presence, or about what a phone will actually offer.
